items.title: Woman’s Bold Biblical Mission to ‘Capture … Souls From Hell’
items.author: Billy Hallowell
items.summary: "I want to see people come to Jesus."
items.content:
📖 News | Faithwire

Ministry leader Bunni Pounds is on a mission to encourage Americans to crack open their Bibles and learn more about the Lord.

Pounds, founder of the newly minted Bunni Pounds Ministries, told CBN News her previous mission of motivating Christians to vote has been replaced by efforts to spark interest in the Bible. Her America Reads the Bible initiative earlier this year ignited Bible interest among millions of people, with three million watching as 500 national leaders read through the entire Bible.

“I’ve spent the last seven years of my life trying to mobilize Christians to pray, vote, engage through Christians Engaged,” she said. “But America Reads the Bible shifted my entire life and our team, and we just realized there’s a root problem more below the surface than just Christians engaging and voting.”

Pounds believes America has a biblical literacy problem. And seeing how America Reads the Bible took form motivated her to seek more of a biblical impact.

“It impacted so many people in this country,” she said of the effort. “And I realized we’ve got to pour gasoline on this. We’ve got to really reach the younger generation, and so we launched the ministry with the idea that we are going to lead thousands of people through a Bible study created with Great American Pure Flix with this content.”

Pounds and her ministry are inviting people to go through the Bible together over a 24-week period starting Jan. 1; she’s calling the effort The Whole Bible Live. Pounds is also planning yet another national event in 2028, along with other local efforts.

“At the end of the day, I want to see people come to Jesus,” Pounds said, explaining what success for her new ministry might look like. “I want to see people be discipled, and I want to see people become disciple makers, and so success looks like hundreds of thousands of people, in the next five years, going through the Bible, becoming the leaders that God’s called them to be, understanding who they truly are in Christ, and taking on the culture, and bringing truth into culture.”

Pounds said young people are hungry and “desperate for God” — and she delivered an important reminder for believers.

“We’re not fighting against people that we disagree with,” she said. “God is after people’s hearts. He’s trying to capture their souls from hell.”

Pounds said she believes America is at a turning point and that Christians need to be encouraging everyone to turn to the Lord. She encouraged people to go to Bunni Pounds Ministries and take part in the Whole Bible Live.

“We need Jesus in this moment,” Pounds said.

items.title: Are Demons Real? New Data Reveals Americans’ Experience With Spiritual Attacks
items.author: Billy Hallowell
items.summary: Wow.
items.content:
📖 News | Faithwire

Spiritual warfare is a real part of the human experience, and the Bible explicitly details how events in the spiritual realm affect people.

“For our struggle is not against flesh and blood, but against the rulers, against the authorities, against the powers of this dark world and against the spiritual forces of evil in the heavenly realms,” Ephesians 6:12 (NIV) reads, with verse 13 continuing: “Therefore put on the full armor of God, so that when the day of evil comes, you may be able to stand your ground, and after you have done everything, to stand.”

The question isn’t if people will experience spiritual warfare; it’s when. A new survey from the American Bible Society (ABS) explores what Americans believe about spiritual warfare, specifically measuring how many people believe they have faced such attacks (watch CBN’s documentary “Investigating the Supernatural: Angels and Demons” today).

Dr. John Plake, editor-in-chief of the State of the Bible series and chief innovation officer at ABS, told CBN News that around 1-in-4 Americans report facing spiritual warfare.

“We saw real difference here across levels of faith participation,” he said. “About a fourth — 26% — of American adults say they’ve had that experience.”

He continued, “[Fifty-eight percent] of practicing Christians would agree with that statement, casual Christians, 28%, nominal Christians, 24%, and then non-Christians, 10%.”

The topic itself is quite fascinating, as Plake said it’s sometimes hard to quantify what a spiritual attack denotes. And since there’s not “a lot of deep data” there’s not qualitative information to help understand what respondents believe a spiritual attack looked like or entailed.

“I’m sure these people do have stories that they can tell about times when they felt like the negative experiences that they were having couldn’t be attributed just to natural causes, that there was some form of spiritual opposition that was going on,” Plake said. “And to see that incidence be that high, I was pretty fascinated by it.”

Another factor ABS was able to screen for was people’s reaction to a perceived spiritual attack — and those statistics were equally interesting.

“So 74% of people who [said they faced attack] said that the way they respond to spiritual attack is that they pray,” Plake said. “I think that makes a lot of sense, right? When spiritual attacks come, you may not be in a particular context where it’s easy to do much else, but you can always pray.”

The second-highest percentage was 36%, who said they declare Christ’s authority.

“There is this kind of sense that … they’re aware they’re in a spiritual battle, that their opposition isn’t … the person who may be opposing them at the moment,” Plake said. “But actually, there’s a spiritual thing going on here, and so they declare Christ’s authority.”

Next came the 24% who said they listen to praise and worship music, but then there’s the smallest — and most concerning — percentage: the 15% who said that they meditate on or quote Scripture.

“I would have hoped that would be a little bit higher,” Plake said. “And I think it also presents an opportunity for pastors and church leaders to recognize, ‘Hey, there are a lot of people, particularly in the church, who are having these experiences, and how can we equip them biblically to respond when they’re facing these kinds of spiritual attacks or moments of opposition, or even when there’s a need for a miraculous healing?'”

For more on this topic, watch “Investigating the Supernatural: Angels and Demons.”

To him, the colonies are British, and the Crown is the source and protector of the very
items.content:
📖 News | Christian Headlines
Benjamin Clem is a teenager in 1770s colonial America who believes in the patriots’ fight for freedom and isn’t afraid to say so to anyone who sides with the British.His brother Jeremiah sees things differently. To him, the colonies are British, and the Crown is the source and protector of the very rights the patriots claim to be fighting for.The brothers might find it easier to live with their differences if they lived apart. Instead, they share a roof with their widowed mother. Their father died on the voyage across the Atlantic when a French vessel attacked the British ship carrying the family.Benjamin and Jeremiah both watched their father die, but they disagree on what he gave his life for.“You betray all he fought for,” Jeremiah tells Benjamin one night at the dinner table as their mother tries to keep the peace.“Father didn't die for England – he died for us,” Benjamin retorts. “He said this was the only place we could truly be free.” “The new world is the same as the old one,” Jeremiah responds. “Father didn't live to see it, but I have.”Soon, the brothers find themselves on opposite sides of the battlefield in the Revolutionary War, each convinced he’s fighting for a just cause and growing more resentful of the other for choosing the opposite side.It’s all part of the new Angel Studios movie Drummer Boy (PG-13), which stars Joel Smallbone of For King & Country as Jeremiah, Lucas Leach as Benjamin,p and Charles Esten (Nashville) as a British officer, Lord Balfour. Smallbone and his brother Luke wrote the music. Another Smallbone, Ben, co-directed it alongside Joel. Here are three reasons families will probably love it:Photo Credit: ©Angel Studios

items.title: Joel Smallbone and the Brother He Drifted From Just Made a Movie About Brothers at War
items.author: Cameron Strang
items.summary: At one point, Joel Smallbone and his brother Ben went their separate ways. “You could argue we ended up on our own sort of opposite sides of life’s battlefield,” Smallbone says. What brought them back together was a movie about the same thing. “I remember saying, wouldn’t it be fascinating if two br
items.content:
📖 Culture | Relevant Magazine

At one point, Joel Smallbone and his brother Ben went their separate ways. “You could argue we ended up on our own sort of opposite sides of life’s battlefield,” Smallbone says. What brought them back together was a movie about the same thing.

“I remember saying, wouldn’t it be fascinating if two brothers who’ve had ideological differences and creative differences came back together behind the camera to tell a story about two brothers that end up on opposite sides of a literal war?”

That movie is Drummer Boy, a Revolutionary War Christmas musical that opened in theaters Nov. 6. Joel and Ben co-directed it, and Joel plays Jeremiah Clem. The cast includes Ioan Gruffudd and Melora Hardin (Jan from The Office).

It took a while. Smallbone, who sings in for KING + COUNTRY with his brother Luke, pitched it to Lionsgate on March 10, 2020, and, by his account, the studio nearly greenlit it.

“And then March the 13th happened and the world shut down,” he says. Unsung Hero came first and the musical waited. Someone eventually reminded him 2026 is America’s 250th birthday. “Well, maybe it was just always meant to be now.”

The Movie That Wrote Him

“Do you write the movie or does the movie write you?” Smallbone asks. “There’s never been a movie that’s written me more than Drummer Boy.”

He lists the evidence. “We came up with this rendition of ‘The Little Drummer Boy’ at the beginning of our career. We’re called for KING + COUNTRY, which is a British mantra. We wore these revolutionary-type uniforms for many years. I’m in a band with my brother. This is a movie about brothers on opposite sides of the battlefield. I’m a musician. It’s a musical. You just see all of these breadcrumbs.”

When he got stuck on the lead character, a director asked him who he was. “I’ve got a rescuer complex,” he says. “A bit of a savior complex. And so I just wrote all of it into the film.”

Unsung Hero was literally about his family, so it’s fair to ask why this one feels more like him. His answer is allegory.

“Jesus was the allegory guy,” Smallbone says. “He made up stories for a living, you know? I see myself more in it because it’s all allegorical about our life, and America, and me being an immigrant and in a mixed marriage, and brothers on other sides of the battlefield.”

A Musical for People Who Hate Musicals

“I need to clear up something to the musical haters,” he says. About 30 minutes of the film are musical moments, “very personal expressions of heartache or love or loss.” He calls it “Hamilton meets The Patriot meets Pride and Prejudice.”

His rule for when a character should sing is simple. “The best musicals put language to things that you couldn’t express through dialogue. The worst musicals just sing the whole time. And I’m like, just stop. That’s not life.”

His example is Chris Martin writing “Fix You” after Gwyneth Paltrow’s father died. “You have to express yourself in grief, in pain, and a lot of times it comes through music.”

The same logic runs through the film. One character, an enslaved woman, sings her way through being stuck. “She’s stuck and she’s enslaved and she needs to sing about it to understand it better,” he says.

Two Brothers Behind the Camera

The shoot gave the co-directing brothers plenty of challenges to overcome. The last day of filming was the big argument between Jeremiah and Emmaline on a hillside, in 40 mph winds.

“She’s in this dress, almost getting blown off the hillside,” Smallbone says. “We were like, I don’t know if we’re gonna use any of this.” The wind made the cut. “The tragedy of the bad weather actually created a third layer to the scene.”

The argument matters to the story. Jeremiah, Smallbone says, is “not practicing what he’s preached.” His father taught him “no boy or girl or slave or free, because all in one in Christ are we,” an echo of Galatians 3:28. Jeremiah is “chasing, basically, imperialism and hierarchy and climbing the ladder by who he’s gonna marry.”

Heat was the opposite problem. On a day he puts at 87 degrees, the Irish cast and crew, who spend winter swimming in a rocky ocean, wilted. “You would have thought we were in New Mexico, or Las Vegas on a hot summer,” he says. “A couple of people were hospitalized.”

Drummer Boy had company on the Irish shoot. Smallbone played a villain in a small role in Young Washington, a film about the young George Washington made there, and he’s at peace with the overlap. He points to something Rick Rubin says: “Don’t be upset if that idea that you thought of comes to life through someone else’s vision. It’s not that they stole your idea, it’s that the time had come for the idea.”

Young Washington paid off for him, too. He kept the red British uniform, he says, and “they let me run onto the sets outside of filming, and they let me borrow one of their featured extras” to shoot a sizzle reel that “ended up helping get Drummer Boy funded.” He wandered the island in character and apologized to anyone who gave him a look. “I’d go, ‘Hey, I’m really sorry. I’m Australian. I’m not even from England.’”

Forgiveness is the theme he says he’s proudest of in the film. “What does it mean to be forgiven by God? What does it mean to forgive yourself? What does it mean to forgive others?” Smallbone asks. “You can’t have freedom without forgiveness.”

It was personal for the Smallbones, too. He and Ben had to find their way back to each other before they could make a movie about it. “It was really Drummer Boy when it came back around,” he says, “and we started talking again.”

items.title: Wisdom Is Seeking You Out
items.author: Bishop Robert Barron
items.summary:
Bishop Robert Barron

Friends, our first reading this Sunday from the book of Wisdom begins, “Resplendent and unfading is wisdom, and she is readily perceived by those who love her, and found by those who seek her.”
items.content:
📖 Catholic Teaching | Word on Fire

Bishop Robert Barron

Friends, our first reading this Sunday from the book of Wisdom begins, “Resplendent and unfading is wisdom, and she is readily perceived by those who love her, and found by those who seek her.” The Bible is preoccupied with the search for wisdom because Jesus is the Wisdom of God made flesh. But to get there, I want to first move step by step through this passage, which lays out an extraordinary vision of the Wisdom of God—a person who not only is sought by us but also seeks us out.

Daily Reading

First Reading
Wisdom 6:12-16

Wisdom is radiant and unfading,
and she is easily discerned by those who love her,
and is found by those who seek her.
She hastens to make herself known to those who desire her.
One who rises early to seek her will have no difficulty,
for she will be found sitting at the gate.
To fix one’s thought on her is perfect understanding,
and one who is vigilant on her account will soon be free from care,
because she goes about seeking those worthy of her,
and she graciously appears to them in their paths,
and meets them in every thought.

Psalm
Psalm 63:2-8

So I have looked upon you in the sanctuary,
    beholding your power and glory.
Because your steadfast love is better than life,
    my lips will praise you.
So I will bless you as long as I live;
    I will lift up my hands and call on your name.
My soul is satisfied as with a rich feast,
    and my mouth praises you with joyful lips
when I think of you on my bed,
    and meditate on you in the watches of the night;
for you have been my help,
    and in the shadow of your wings I sing for joy.
My soul clings to you;
    your right hand upholds me.

Second Reading
1 Thessalonians 4:13-18

But we do not want you to be uninformed, brothers and sisters, about those who have died, so that you may not grieve as others do who have no hope. For since we believe that Jesus died and rose again, even so, through Jesus, God will bring with him those who have died. For this we declare to you by the word of the Lord, that we who are alive, who are left until the coming of the Lord, will by no means precede those who have died. For the Lord himself, with a cry of command, with the archangel’s call and with the sound of God’s trumpet, will descend from heaven, and the dead in Christ will rise first. Then we who are alive, who are left, will be caught up in the clouds together with them to meet the Lord in the air; and so we will be with the Lord forever. Therefore encourage one another with these words.

Gospel Reading
Matthew 25:1-13

“Then the kingdom of heaven will be like this. Ten bridesmaids took their lamps and went to meet the bridegroom. Five of them were foolish, and five were wise. When the foolish took their lamps, they took no oil with them; but the wise took flasks of oil with their lamps. As the bridegroom was delayed, all of them became drowsy and slept. But at midnight there was a shout, ‘Look! Here is the bridegroom! Come out to meet him.’ Then all those bridesmaids got up and trimmed their lamps. The foolish said to the wise, ‘Give us some of your oil, for our lamps are going out.’ But the wise replied, ‘No! there will not be enough for you and for us; you had better go to the dealers and buy some for yourselves.’ And while they went to buy it, the bridegroom came, and those who were ready went with him into the wedding banquet; and the door was shut. Later the other bridesmaids came also, saying, ‘Lord, lord, open to us.’ But he replied, ‘Truly I tell you, I do not know you.’ Keep awake therefore, for you know neither the day nor the hour.

items.title: ‘Babette’s Feast’ and the Healing Power of Eros
items.author: Lydia Perri
items.summary:
Lydia Perri

True feasting is not a profane indulgence of the senses, but a cosmological affirmation: The world is good, and it is good that I exist in it.
items.content:
📖 Catholic Teaching | Word on Fire

Lydia Perri

In a remote village on the windswept coast of Jutland, there lived the pious spinster sisters, Martine and Filippa. Thus begins the 1987 Academy Award-winning film Babette’s Feast, a film in which very little happens on the surface—people eat soup, sing hymns, and occasionally glare at one another—yet beneath that rolls an emotional and spiritual tidal wave. 

In this little corner of the world, one of the four loves, eros, has been systematically repressed by the sisters’ father, the Dean, in his pietistic congregation. But eros, classically understood, is not mere sexual appetite. It is a life force: the passionate longing to be satiated in beauty, connection, creativity, sensual fulfillment, and perfect happiness. Rather than being a flaw in our fallen nature, it is part of God’s design to bring us to himself. In Babette’s Feast, this love is briefly awakened (though misdirected) in the sisters’ youth until it is finally fulfilled when joined to Babette’s total self-gift. Through her feast, the villagers—long stunted, resentful, and suspicious in their limited understanding of Christian love—discover the healing power of eros.

Martine and Filippa, named for Martin Luther and Philip Melanchthon, live their days doing good deeds and presiding over the congregation left by their late father. The villagers are tightly knit, and the sisters’ love for those around them is genuinely charitable and dutiful. Yet theirs is an incomplete love, carefully scrubbed of anything that might be mistaken for pleasure: the villagers wear drab gray and black clothing, their daily fare consists of salted fish and boiled ale-bread soup, and they gather every Sunday in a plain white chapel in a bare service of hymn singing and a simple sermon. The village essentially operates under a perpetual fast, starving the senses in order to feed the spirit. Any divergence from this fast is treated as tantamount to apostasy. Yet when God saw his creation, he declared it very good. Our bodies and senses are the sacramental pathways of his grace. 

Forty-nine years before the opening of the film, the sisters had suitors in the dashing leonine cavalry officer Lorens Löwenhielm and the renowned Parisian baritone Achille Papin. Following the storytelling law that “nomen est omen,” their names carry suggestive layers of meaning. Lorens, whose name literally means “a crowned lion in armor,” is struck by Martine’s “almost supernatural fairness” and hopes she might tame his hunger for gambling and drink. A shared life with her might have led him to greatness of soul. But a lion’s appetite for vainglory and greatness cannot be satiated in the quiet humble life in the village. He flees back to the city to hunt for status, eventually marrying into the royal court and rising to the rank of general. Lorens’s hunger for greatness is legitimate, yet he abandons the path that might have purified it. Martine, whose soul is briefly stirred by attraction, counts his departure a blessing that preserves their careful control of the passions.

Achille Papin’s name is an echo of the great Greek warrior Achilles, while his surname, Papin, historically implies “soft nursery food”—an ironic “soft Achilles.” He arrives on a sort of sabbatical after the Parisian life of glory and artistic passion has left him feeling empty. The glittering lights of the stage and adoring audiences, directed inward instead of upward toward the Artist himself, prove hollow. Hearing Filippa’s angelic singing in the Dean’s church, he obtains permission to tutor her in opera. Achille’s artistic passion rekindles, and it seems as though there might be a flame between himself and Filippa. Alas, while practicing Don Giovanni, Achille succumbs to the emotion of the scene and kisses Filippa. His eros has not been disciplined. For Filippa, the awakened passions are too awful, and she breaks off their tutelage. She is startled less by Achille’s actions than her own latent response. Both men sought eros, but failed to direct it toward its proper end. The sisters, lacking the language to discuss such desires, simply suppress them.

Thirty-five years later, in blows the refugee Babette, soaked to the bone by a squalling tempest. Her name, the French diminutive of Barbara, derives from the Greek barbaros, meaning foreign, strange. In mythology, the “stranger” who asks for refuge is often a disguised divine messenger who tests the hospitality of those he visits. Babette carries a letter from the aged Achille Papin explaining that she has just escaped persecution by the Paris Commune and recommending her as a housekeeper. In a line of hilarious understatement, he notes that she “can cook.” 

The sisters have nothing to give in compensation, but Babette insists that she work for free or will die if turned away. Over the next fourteen years, Babette wins her way into the villagers’ grudging hearts. She produces improved ale-bread soup and cleverly manages the sisters’ finances so they have more to give in charity to the community. Because Babette brings into the village neither Lorens’s restless ambition nor Papin’s emotional excess but an eros already disciplined by love, she gains their trust. But as the years slip by and their austere band dwindles, the community shows growing fractures. Love, when reduced down to service, has become sterile.

All that changes as the centenary of the late Dean’s birth approaches. Babette learns she has won a lottery of 10,000 francs. To the sisters’ shock and unease, Babette begs them to allow her to use her new fortune to cook an authentic Parisian feast for the centenary celebration. Out of love and respect for Babette, they nervously agree. 

Over the next few weeks, Babette imports everything from France. This time, eros arrives not in the overt sensuality of Papin but in wheelbarrows of sea turtle, cow’s head, and cages of quails. Such exotic preparations horrify the sisters and other villagers. Their resolution is the most entertaining irony of the film: They will eat the food served to them, but will make no comment about its pleasures, essentially receiving a gift while refusing to delight in it. It shall be to them as all their daily fare: simply nourishment for the body, nothing more.

The dinner party numbers twelve, including Lorens Löwenhielm. From a worldly perspective, he has achieved impressive success, yet he admits to himself that he feels empty. During the feast, Babette herself remains in the kitchen, overseeing her great masterpiece. As dish after dish of exquisite food is laid before them, Lorens offers educated commentary while the congregants smile and act as if he were discussing the weather. Despite themselves, however, the congregants have begun to lower their defenses. Spontaneously, forgiveness for past foibles and resentments flows as freely as the wine. Over the many courses, decades-old quarrels are reconciled, and the meal ends in laughter. Outside under the stars, they join hands and circle the village well. 

When the sisters return to Babette, they are shocked to learn she spent her entire 10,000-franc fortune on that one meal for them. But in Babette’s words, “An artist is never poor.” Babette’s secret is that she possesses erotic love in its full artistic sense, that passionate longing to create a beauty that does not terminate in itself. She elevates her eros and unites it to agape precisely because she spends everything to give that beauty to others. Her self-gift is simultaneously extravagant and disciplined, sensual and spiritual, personally fulfilling and wholly generous. Babette’s feast becomes an anticipation of the beatific vision, the heavenly banquet of the Lamb, because material abundance serves as a direct channel of forgiveness and communion. This union of loves finally breaks open the hearts of the late Dean’s congregation to divine mercy and the life of grace. 

Although the villagers had the right instinct to place love of God above all other goods, their mistake was to fall into a quasi-Gnostic error that treats material goods as treacherous to salvation. Earthly joys become illusions at best, and at worst, dangers to be renounced for the sake of the purely heavenly Jerusalem. The perpetual fast that resulted is unbiblical and diminishes Christian life, hence the dwindling community, unresolved grudges, culture of suspicion, and a loss of joy. The answer is neither indulgence nor suppression but conversion. How can we believe in an incarnate Christ and deny the goodness of his creation? We ought to recognize created beauty as a gift and ascend through that beauty to its source. Even the most austere, monastic communities acknowledge the importance of the feast after the fast. As twentieth-century German Catholic philosopher Josef Pieper explains in both In Tune with the World: A Theory of Festivity and Leisure: The Basis of Culture, true feasting is not a profane indulgence of the senses, but a cosmological affirmation: The world is good, and it is good that I exist in it.

True, the human act of feasting as an overflow of existential richness requires a structural relationship with fasting to avoid degrading into mere consumption. Because human desire is wounded by concupiscence, the physical pleasures of food, wine, marital intimacy, and art easily become idols when not guided by the virtues of temperance and wisdom. True asceticism denies the body temporarily in order to strengthen the soul, while never denying the goodness of the body or other earthly goods. The conscious practice of saying no on occasion leads to a deeper yes to God.

The infinite hunger of eros for particular earthly pleasures is meant to lead beyond them. Physical joys are a sensory foretaste of the ultimate human end: the beatific vision. Like the angel in St. Teresa of Avila’s ecstasy, Babette’s feast pierces the dinner guests with an arrow that reconciles body and spirit. Eros is generative, leading to wisdom, honor, children (in the natural order), and spiritual fruit. Disordered desire isolates or destroys; ordered desire integrates body and soul, individual and community. The ascent becomes a real sharing in God’s beauty and love. Eros is purified and fulfilled in self-gift; agape is passionate and attractive through eros.
